query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled powder‐bed/substrate pre‐heat during laser powder bed fusion of AlCrFeNiSi feedstock will reduce thermal gradients during processing, thereby minimizing residual thermal stresses, promoting a more uniform microstructure, and improving the mechanical properties of miniature components relative to those produced under conventional room-temperature, high‐thermal‐load conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-alloyed AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with typical particle size distribution used in metallic AM.
generation.intervention: Implement a process modification whereby the build platform (and optionally the surrounding powder bed) is maintained at an elevated temperature (e.g., in the range of approximately 300°C–500°C) throughout deposition during laser powder bed fusion.
generation.conditions: Processing miniature components (e.g., tensile test coupons or small lattice structures) using LPBF; the processing window involves standard laser parameters used for this feedstock but with the additional pre-heating condition; tests carried out under controlled inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; geometric features typical of miniature additively manufactured parts.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduced thermal gradient along the build direction, leading to moderated cooling rates and diminished thermal contraction differentials between layers, which in turn fosters a more homogeneous microstructure with minimized residual stress accumulation.
generation.mechanism: Pre-heating the build platform minimizes the differential cooling rates and thermal contractions between successive layers. This reduced temperature gradient decreases the formation of high residual stresses and associated microstructural defects during rapid solidification. As a result, the mechanical integrity (e.g., microhardness, tensile strength) is expected to improve over parts built under conventional, room-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to components manufactured under standard high-thermal-load conditions, pre-heated builds will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in residual thermal stress levels and demonstrate enhanced mechanical properties, such as increased microhardness and improved tensile performance.
generation.baseline: Specimens produced using conventional LPBF at room temperature (i.e., without substrate/powder bed pre-heating) that typically suffer from high residual stresses and degraded mechanical properties due to rapid thermal cycling.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the pre-heating intervention may be confined to the scale of miniature components where the thermal mass is low and controlled pre-heating can be uniformly applied. Scaling to larger components or different alloy compositions may require additional parameter optimization.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by general principles of thermal stress management in additive manufacturing, the precise pre-heating temperature window and the quantitative improvement in mechanical properties for AlCrFeNiSi feedstock remain to be determined through dedicated experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature test components (e.g., standardized tensile or microhardness test coupons) using the same AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock via LPBF. One set is manufactured under conventional, room-temperature conditions, while the other set is built with the build platform pre-heated to a target temperature (e.g., 400°C) within the identified processing window. Ensure all other processing parameters (laser power, scan speed, atmosphere) are identical. After fabrication, measure the residual stress levels using X-ray diffraction, characterize the microstructure via SEM/TEM, and perform mechanical testing (microhardness, tensile testing).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-heated components do not show statistically significant improvements (beyond the experimental uncertainty) in both reduced residual stress levels and enhanced mechanical properties relative to the conventional components, the hypothesis that pre-heating mitigates the adverse effects of high thermal gradients in this alloy system will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
